description: Reference data for TFF Training Plan Skill. Question sequence is defined in SKILL.md — this file contains options, formulas and validation details only.
hr_zones_source_options: Yes — lab test (spiroergometry / lactate threshold test)
Yes — field test (20-min max effort test)
Yes — device estimate (Garmin, Polar, etc.) — note: may be off by 10-20 bpm
No — calculate from my age and resting HR

hr_zone_calculation._warning: The two methods below use the same percentage bands but those percentages refer to DIFFERENT quantities: Karvonen percentages are % of heart rate reserve (% HRR), age_based percentages are % of maximum HR (% max HR). They are not interchangeable. Example — age 42, resting HR 58, Tanaka max HR 179: Z2 at 60-70% HRR = 130-142 bpm, while 60-70% of max HR = 107-125 bpm (23 bpm apart, roughly a full zone). Always label the percentage column in the plan with the method actually used, and tell the user the bpm values are what they enter into their device.

karvonen.percent_of: heart rate reserve (% HRR) — label the column '% HRR (Karvonen)'
karvonen.max_hr_note: Tanaka et al. 2001 (JACC) — meta-analysis of 351 studies, >18,000 subjects. More accurate than 220-age, which overestimates in younger adults and underestimates with increasing age (~10 bpm difference at age 70).
karvonen.formula: Zone bpm = Resting HR + (% × (Max HR - Resting HR))

age_based.percent_of: maximum HR (% max HR) — label the column '% max HR'

examples._note: These examples illustrate correct assumption-stating behavior and output constraints. Reference these when applying Rule 16 (assumption transparency) and the complementary-declined case.

running_partial_info_pace_unknown.scenario: User provides goal, age, days, and duration but does not mention current 5k time or pace.
running_partial_info_pace_unknown.correct_behavior: State the assumption explicitly before proceeding. Do NOT silently estimate. Example output: 'You didn't mention your current pace — based on your intermediate fitness level, I'll estimate your easy pace at ~7:00/km (from the assessment reference table). I'll note this in the plan and you should adjust after your first session if it feels off.' Then continue with the next block.

strength_complementary_declined.scenario: User explicitly declines complementary cardio when asked in Block 5.
strength_complementary_declined.correct_behavior: Accept the answer and proceed to plan generation. At the very end of the completed plan (after all weekly sessions are shown), add exactly ONE line: 'Note: Adding 10 min of calf and hip stability work per week significantly reduces injury risk — recommended if you change your mind.' Do NOT add any other references to complementary training, cardio sessions, or injury prevention notes anywhere else in the plan body.

pace_estimation_when_unknown._instruction: Use these ranges ONLY when the user has no race data. If a recent race time is known, derive paces from it via goals/runner.md Principle 2c (Riegel + race-pace offsets) instead — that is the more accurate path. Always state the estimate clearly. The bands are the expected range for a level, not a floor: if the user's real pace sits outside the band, say that the level label and the pace disagree and ask for a recent run rather than forcing the estimate back inside.
pace_estimation_when_unknown._consistency: These values must stay identical to the estimation table in goals/runner.md Principle 2b.
pace_estimation_when_unknown._source: Coaching heuristic calibrated against the spread of recreational finisher times. NOT a measurement and NOT a literature finding — unlike Tanaka (max HR), Riegel (race-time equivalence) and Lauersen (injury reduction), these bands have no primary source, because none exists for 'what pace does an intermediate runner hold'. Present them as a starting bracket the first two weeks will correct, never as a norm the user should measure themselves against.

beginner.note: Decide walk-run versus continuous from how long the user can currently run without stopping and what they have recently tolerated, not from the estimated pace. Use the lower end of the range if they report running continuously.

intermediate.note: Running continuously, building aerobic base. If the user's actual easy pace sits outside this band, the label and the pace disagree — ask for a recent run instead of moving the estimate.

advanced.note: Consistent training history, race experience likely.
